Consult Summary:
- 31-year-old woman with ~2 months of progressive anxiety centered on a new work role, causing significant morning dread, daytime impairment, low mood, reduced enjoyment of activities, and insomnia.
- Palpitations described as irregular, episodic, and associated with morning panic; clinician impression: anxiety-related palpitations but recommended basic blood tests and GP follow-up.

Problem List:

Issue 1: Anxiety related to work (presenting problem)
- Timeline/progression: Symptoms began approximately 2 months ago, coinciding with starting a new job in retail head office; progressive worsening.
- Core symptoms: Persistent excessive worry about work, morning dread about leaving the house, anticipatory anxiety about performance and interactions with a difficult boss, avoidance of social activities at times, reduced enjoyment of previously enjoyed activities.
- Functional impact: Impaired sleep, low daytime energy, decreased participation in hobbies (running, tennis), difficulty relaxing, thinks about calling in sick frequently but continues to attend work.
- Psychiatric review: No prior similar episodes reported; denies suicidal ideation or intent. Mother has history of depression.
- Social/other relevant: Lives with parents; has family support.
- Specialist/allied health: Offered self-referral to NHS talking therapies (one-to-one therapy); clinician to send referral/link and online resources.

Issue 2: Insomnia / sleep disturbance (secondary to anxiety)
- Timeline: Ongoing for ~2 months with worsening sleep.
- Symptoms: Difficulty falling asleep (lying awake for hours), very shallow sleep, estimated 3–4 hours total sleep, frequent early awakening with panic and racing heart.
- Daytime effects: Low energy, anhedonia, impaired functioning.
- Management discussed: Clinician to add information on sleep hygiene to notes; encouraged use of online resources and talking therapy; medication not offered as first-line.

Issue 3: Palpitations (episodes likely anxiety-related)
- Characteristics: Irregular, rapid heartbeats occurring most often in the morning with onset of panic or fear of being late; duration variable (minutes up to ~10 minutes).
- Associated symptoms: No chest pain reported beyond discomfort from strong palpitations; no syncope.
- Clinician impression: Most likely associated with anxiety but recommended basic blood tests to exclude physiological triggers.
- Management: Patient advised to contact support line to arrange blood tests; arrange GP follow-up approximately one week after blood tests to review results. No cardiac investigations (ECG) documented in transcript.

Medications:
- No regular medications reported.
- Clinician discussed possibility of medication for anxiety in the future but none started.

Allergies:
- No allergies reported in the consult.

Past Medical History:
- None reported in the transcript.

Social History:
- Lives with parents.
- Alcohol: Patient reports drinking “quite a lot” on Fridays/Saturdays and possibly a glass during the week when offered by parents; exact amounts not quantified.
- Tobacco: Occasional smoker (“try not to smoke, but I do occasionally”).
- Recreational drugs: Denies use.
- Employment: New job in fashion retail head office; work stressor identified as principal trigger.

Preventative History:
- No preventative care items (cervical screening, mammogram, PSA, FOBT, bone density, vaccinations, optometry, skin check) documented.

Physical Examination:
- No vital signs or physical examination findings documented in the transcript.

Plan:
- Immediate:
  - Provide patient with NHS talking-therapy self-referral link and online resources for anxiety and sleep hygiene.
  - Patient to contact support line to arrange basic blood tests as recommended.
- Short-term follow-up:
  - GP follow-up appointment arranged approximately 1 week after blood tests to review results and reassess symptoms.
  - Patient advised to contact clinic earlier if anxiety worsens, she becomes unable to cope with work or daily activities, or if suicidal ideation develops.
- Longer-term:
  - Offer one-to-one psychotherapy (cognitive/behavioral approaches) as first-line.
  - Consider pharmacologic treatment later if therapy and self-help measures are insufficient (discussed but not started).

Document_quality / Quality checks:
- Missing but clinically expected elements:
  - Vital signs (heart rate, blood pressure, temperature).
  - Physical examination findings.
  - Specific blood tests ordered (which tests and rationale) and any planned cardiac investigations (ECG) — not specified.
  - Exact alcohol units and smoking frequency.
  - Medication reconciliation and past medical history details beyond what patient volunteered.
- Internal conflicts from transcript:
  - None significant; patient statements are consistent. (Patient initially said “I try not to smoke” and later confirmed occasional smoking — consistent.)
- Transcript quality:
  - Conversation intelligible and sufficiently detailed; few pauses and some colloquial speech but clinically relevant information clearly documented.
